definition: Derivative-free optimization (sometimes referred to as blackbox optimization) is a discipline in mathematical optimization that does not use derivative information in the classical sense to find optimal solutions: Sometimes information about the derivative of the objective function f is unavailable, unreliable or impractical to obtain.
details: For example, f might be non-smooth, or time-consuming to evaluate, or in some way noisy, so that methods that rely on derivatives or approximate them via finite differences are of little use. The problem to find optimal points in such situations is referred to as derivative-free optimization, algorithms that do not use derivatives or finite differences are called derivative-free algorithms.

explainer.lead: Derivative-free optimization searches for a good solution without using derivatives of the objective function. It matters when those derivatives are unavailable, unreliable, or too impractical to obtain—for example because evaluations are noisy or time-consuming.

tiers.eli5: When you cannot tell which way is downhill, you still try points and keep the ones that work better.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply these methods when the objective is a black box, such as a slow simulation or a noisy process. The pitfall is that avoiding derivatives usually costs many more function evaluations.
tiers.paperLevel: Optimization of an objective f without derivatives or finite-difference approximations; the problem is called derivative-free (or blackbox) optimization, and algorithms that use neither are derivative-free algorithms. Such methods are typically sample-hungry.

explainer.example: Suppose f(x1, x2) takes an hour to evaluate and returns noisy results, making finite differences impractical. Start by evaluating (2, 5), then try other candidate pairs, compare their observed values, and continue around promising settings while keeping the best result observed.
explainer.intuition: Instead of asking which direction a derivative points in, learn from the objective values at points you actually try. Each evaluation supplies evidence for choosing subsequent candidates.
howItWorks: Choose one or more candidate input points.
Evaluate the objective f at those points.
Use the observations to propose new candidates.
Repeat and retain the best point found.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a way to optimize objectives when gradient-based methods and finite-difference approximations are of little use. This makes optimization possible even when each evaluation is noisy, non-smooth, or costly.
misconceptions: Derivative-free does not mean evaluation-free: the objective must still be evaluated at candidate points.
Finite differences are not included; the definition excludes algorithms that use them to approximate derivatives.
Noisy observations can make the best observed point differ from the true optimum.
